Agent Walker manages to pass the threshold of being enjoyable (mostly thanks to its visual presentation), but with large warning signs for its disjointed story, childishly simple puzzles, and strangely overcrowded hidden object scenes.

[h1]Long version:[/h1]
The hidden object games made by Brave Giant tend to be small hits or big misses—Agent Walker: Secret Journey sits somewhere between those, in a rather uncomfortable position.
Theoretically, this game should be awesome: set in the middle of the World War II, we play as an agent sent on a mission to retrieve the Spear of Destiny before the Axis does. However, the premise quickly falls apart under the myriads of few-second video clips that have little connection to each other, completely killing any flow the story could have had.

Gameplay also show some concerning duality: the hidden object scenes are overcrowded and pretty challenging, but the conventional puzzles, including the point ‘n’ click style item hunting, are insultingly easy. I understand that this is a casual genre, but Agent Walker is just a tiny step away of dragging along the player instead of letting them do anything that resembles gameplay.

Even though the story is kinda different from other Artifex Mundi games and is a pretty interesting subject to me... don't think I've ever played any Artifex Mundi hidden object game that happened during WWII. Pretty interesting to explore myths from the era as a theme for these types of games I guess. This one is about the Spear of Destiny, and it has been around in pop culture, comics, animes and others. The specific name spear of destiny I remember mostly from the sequel to the original Wolfenstein game, but it has also been around from it's various other names - lance of God, holy lance, lance of Longuinus... it's the lance that pierce Jesus' flank during the crucifixion.

So, back to the game - the graphics are ok, they seem on par with the newer crop, no weird perspective, resolution and shapes.
Mechanics for hidden object parts are also ok, with the newer stuff like finding and using objects in the same scene, hidden compartments, and the usual stuff hidden behind objects which I don't particularly like, but it's extra instead of just plain hidden objects, so it helps not getting too tiring.

The thing this one suffers like a few other Artifex Mundi games are parts of the scene to zoom in that are too close to each other or kinda hidden, and objects that you have to pick on a scene that is hidden away, stashed in a corner, or just not visible enough, put purposedly in a dark corner.

It is very frustrating to enter a scene with a whole ton of stuff going on that you cannot interact with, but then they hide some ladder or something in some corner not being a hidden object part just so you keep looking after it like an idiot. I think they stopped doing this in more recent games, and I can see why... hidden objects work when it's limited to their specific part, but not if it's just a handful strewn around regular scenes with no clue and no visual cue that you should be looking for them in the first place.

Kinda lazy to make the game difficult that way. Most of the game is ok, but I just don't like when Artifex Mundi devs do stuff like this. I dunno about other players, but at least for me the whole thing about these types of game is flow and going with the story. If there are parts purposedly made for you to get stuck, it damages both the flow and the story, because you get fed up with it and leave it to play some other day, which interrupts the whole thing.

That aside, on this particular title passing through the middle of the game you'll get a long stream of hidden object parts almost like one after the other. It's characteristic of earlier titles too. Depends if you like them or not, but there is a whole lot on this one.

I'm gonna recommend with these caveats in mind... there are far worse titles out there, Artifex Mundi ones are still the standard to beat so far in my personal experience. Just that the mechanics aren't as great as newer titles, despite me liking the story subject...

During World War II, a course to retrieve the mythical Spear of Destiny, destined to help people rule the world, is happening between Axis and Allies. Agent Walker is sent to destroy it after it was localized in France. However, once there, she fell in a trap...

The Spear of Destiny... it's not the first time that I've heard about it: another casual adventure game has the same object in a similar setting and I still remember that a similar artifact was one of the objectives of Lara Croft in Chronicles.

Agent Walker is another twist: while the Spear is found early, Nazis managed to retrieve it as she fell into a trap. The result is the chase through a village and underground temples. However, the Spear of Destiny isn't the only thing: there is a colossus you need to finish as it's protecting the Spear and the machine that can destroy it is situated elsewhere. Some twists are also present, though I would have preferrd more interaction with enemies and more explanations on the twist.

However, Agent Walker is pretty standard on the gameplay: hidden objects scenes to clear (relatively easy, though some items are changing appearance), puzzles (also easy), find items, combine them, use them to advance. Some of the scenes are also with silhouettes to find and to use (without forgetting the only puzzle thrown into the scene).

The graphics are good, but I would have preferred more World War II-related things: I could imagine Agent Walker captured or travelling across Europe or even more confrontation with the real enemy. The soundtrack is good too.

[u]Recommendation[/u]: a decent-but-bonkers hidden object game that blends story elements of Castle Wolfenstein, Agent Carter, and Indiana Jones.

[u]Critique[/u]: This game is at the lower end of the graphics spectrum for Artifex Mundi hidden object games. Textures vary wildly in quality, with some items being hand drawn, some being scanned photos, and some being 3D renders...and they are usually not blended particularly well. 

The voice actors give surprisingly good deliveries, though the speech of the characters (French, German, English, American) all sound like Americans making uneven attempts at other accents (they're often VERY CLOSE to getting it right, but they'll pronounce one key word incorrectly, giving away that they're natively American English speakers). 

The hidden object puzzles are entertaining, often because the size of the objects you're looking for are actually much larger than you expect: sometimes the last object you're trying to find actually takes up a full tenth of the screen - "so large that I didn't see it!" This is abetted by the fact that perspective goes out the window with these hidden object scenes, so a briefcase might appear relatively smaller than a chisel. This leads you to look for really small and/or really dark items (some of the smaller items are hidden as dark grey items in black shadows, so they're very hard to spot). 

The other mini-games are all interesting - some of them are unique to this game, which is always exciting! - but this uniqueness adds difficulty, because you don't always know what you're supposed to do in a given mini-game, even with the instructions that are helpfully provided with EVERY mini-game. 

The game is rated Teen because it is very violent. Yes, you get to beat up Nazis, but in this game the violence is almost comically over-the-top. [spoiler]You straight-up murder nearly every Nazi you see, and often in the most outlandish overkill possible. Two stand-out examples: instead of using a gun or a knife, you engineer a trap to electrocute one, and in another instance, you take the time to assemble and load a bazooka to blow up the Nazi instead of just hitting him with a club.[/spoiler] 

The plot is a fun bit of nonsense: an Indiana Jones-type story of keeping powerful supernatural relics out of the hands of the Third Reich, but a LOT of the individual steps in that plot make very little sense. "Oh, I guess that's happening now," you say as a player again and again when something apparently unrelated to what came before happens. This is not at all unique to this game, of course.

The achievements for the game, thankfully, can all be accomplished in a single play-through of the game, though you have to be on the lookout on all the wide location screens (as opposed to zoomed-in views of specific areas) for a HUGE array of WWII-related items: soldier uniform caps, little wooden figures of historical VIPs, boats, bombs, planes, cannons, and more things that are unrelated to the plot or the locations. It's a lot, but as long as you know that you are looking for them from the start, you can find them all. You DO need to be conscientious about the search, though: the game takes place in several "stages," each consisting of several locations. Once you advance to the next stage, you can never go back to a previous one. So if you miss one of these random items, you won't get all the achievements.

[b][u]Game Information[/u][/b]

"Agent Walker: Secret Journey" is a Hidden Object Puzzle Adventure game. The game was developed by Brave Giant Studio and published by Artifex Mundi.

[b][u]The Game Review[/u][/b]

Game Visuals

I want to mention that the visuals in the game are nicely done. The visuals can be adjusted in the game's option menu.

Game Audio

I want to mention that audio for the game is well done. Even though the audio is somewhat simplistic and repetitive. The audio can be adjusted in the game's option menu as well.

Gameplay

There are four different game difficulty modes to choose from: Casual; Advanced; Expert and Custom.

The notebook keeps track of the progression in the game. Such as story events and clues.

There is an interactive map in the game. It allows the player to fast travel between each location quickly without having the need to constantly backtrack. It also indicates that there are a variety of tasks that can be completed at various locations within the game. The interactive map is automatically given at the start of the game.

There is no padlock feature that is available to lock the inventory panel in place to make it stationary. The inventory panel automatically comes stationary.

There are some interactive items in the game. Some of the interactive items may require extra components before they can be interacted with. All interactive items are marked with a symbol in one of the corners.

The hidden object scenes consist of the following: Find 'x' amount; Shadow items and Traditional word lists. Some of these hidden object scenes may require a little or no interaction. Most of the hidden object scenes can be replayed in the game's extra feature section.

The puzzles are fairly easy to solve without having the need to skip any of them. Most of the puzzles can be replayed in the game's extra feature section as well.

There are three sets of collectibles in the game: Military Uniforms; Doll Figurines; Miniatures. All of the collectibles are scattered throughout the game for the player to find.

There are sixteen different achievements that can be unlocked from playing the game. Each of these achievements does come with some requirements that need to be completed before they can be unlocked.

Miscellaneous

There are extra features in the game: Wallpapers; Interview; Concept Art; Soundtracks; Mini-Games and Hidden Object Scenes. Most of these extra features can be accessed only after the entire game is completed.

There are five different trading cards to collect. Only three of those trading cards are given out by the game. There are several ways to get the rest of the trading cards: Purchased from the Steam's Community Market; Trade with friends; Booster Packs and its Booster Pack Creator.

Final thoughts: I have found the game enjoyable to a certain extent. The replay value for the game is low. I would recommend this game, but not at the game's full price value.

This was definitely a very interesting game, and not what I had initially though it was.  Just from looking at the title, I had assumed that the game was about a secret agent going around in modern times to try and solve a mystery, but I was pleasantly surprised to find out that this took place during WWII.  

The game follows Agent Walker as she goes around trying to find a particular magical item that could change the course of the war.  Of course the Axis is there, trying to get the Spear from you at every turn in the game, but then again, if they weren't there, there would be no opposing force to get it from you.

I really enjoyed how the setting took place during this time period, and how each of the settings were incorporated into each other, like the magical cave in the beginning was hidden away near a mineshaft.  All the artwork and the designs were done beautifully and it is easy to tell a lot of time went into making them.  The environments and settings were broken up into different sections, and there would be sections to the game where you can't back track.  It would make it much easier to focus on just a few different areas instead of a plethora of places you can backtrack to and keep track of. 

Of course that meant that you had to be vigilant about the collectibles in the game since there would be parts you couldn't return to, but it made it all the more worthwhile to get them all.  I really enjoyed how there were figurines, items like the boats and the airplanes you could collect, and you could find different pieces to the actual uniforms.  That made it very unique, and I actually really enjoyed getting to see what each uniform looked like when they were completed.  

The actual Hidden Object games also had variations as well.  Like in the beginning, the first Hidden Object game had you click items to gather crystals to get the Spear, but sometimes it would have you collect pieces of a puzzle or something similar.  The variation definitely helped to make things seem less monotonous, and added a bit more to the plot and the difference in setting.  

The ending to the game was definitely surprising.  Everything went well and the mission was completed, but this is the first time I have ever come across a game where the main character's safety wasn't guaranteed, and it is implied that she had given her life to destroy this item.  Given the time period, it is very likely to have happened, and made this much more different than other games since most games end on a happy note with all the characters surviving.

Overall, it is a very good game and I would recommend playing it.  Well worth the price you pay for it.

As a fan of hidden object games I jump into each one with a sense of excitement and hope, sometimes the game delivers and sometimes it doesn’t. I found [i]Agent Walker: Secret Journey[/i] to be very middle of the road. It had a nice look, nice puzzles and hidden object scenes but lacked an engaging story. This title is one of six currently available on Steam by Brave Giant LTD, so far I’ve played five of these titles and found most to be mediocre. It wasn’t until I played this game the second time that I really noticed it. However, being mediocre doesn’t make this title bad.

The story is set during World War II, you play as Agent Walker, who has been sent on a mission to find a powerful artifact so that the enemy doesn’t get to it first. This MacGuffin is the Spear of Destiny -reputed to be the weapon that killed Jesus Christ, ending his agony on the crucifix.  Some legends declared its wielder became ruler of the world.  It ends up falling into enemy hands as you could imagine and you spend most of the game trying to track it down and destroy it. That’s pretty much all the story is about. Agent Walker is never given any development, she’s a total placeholder for the player with little personality. Despite being set during World War II there is never a huge sense of dread or urgency about anything, this could have easily been set during any war on any planet with the same outcome. There also isn’t much of a supernatural element to the game, there is a brief explanation about the spear given to you during a mini game and not much else. I did find the title to have a decent sense of action though as you do move around often and explore quite a few locations.

What I enjoyed most was the gameplay here, there are plenty of hidden object scenes and puzzles to keep you entertained. The game starts off strong, adding some rarely seen variety to the usual hidden object scenes but that dies off around midway through and they all end up being the usual list of objects you have to find. The scenes do offer morphing objects, this is when an item you need to find continually morphs into another object so you have to keep an eye out when to click on it. The puzzles were enjoyable, most weren’t too difficult at all. There were some fun ones like parachuting and even driving a boat which I don’t often see as well some of the staples you tend to find in this genre. You’re given a map that shows you where an action can be performed and also allows you to teleport, as well as three different difficulty settings and a custom setting.

Visually the game performs well. While some of the animations of the characters might seem a bit stiff, everything looks pretty good. It feels like the 1940’s and like it’s set during a war. The hidden object scenes are done well, the items aren’t hard to see or blurry and overall everything is very clean. The audio, on the other hand, is a mixed bag. Most of the voice acting is pretty lackluster. Some characters speak like robots almost, most are just middle of the road and Agent Walker herself never speaks at all. Voice acting isn’t required, but if you choose to add it, then it should be enjoyable to the ear. Thankfully the music is alright and fits well with the tone and setting of the game.

[i]Agent Walker: Secret Journey[/i] is a good game but it skirts that line. It offers pretty graphics and solid gameplay but if you enjoy a good story you may find yourself disappointed. If you play the game on Steam it does have trading cards and easy to gather achievements if you’re a fan of those. This game was only published by Artifex Mundi so don’t go into it expecting what you might find in some of their other titles, however I do recommend this title if you find it on sale or bundled but it’s rather short for the price tag and offers no bonus chapter and not much extra content. My first run through the game took less than three hours, three enjoyable hours but I wish the game was longer.

Even the collectables are all themed to World War II, there are uniform pieces, small statues (of Hitler, Staline etc) and war figurines to find (planes, war ships etc). 

Sure it’s not designed for small kids, but at least it’s different and it’s rather well done: beautiful crisp graphics, nice music, pretty uncluttered HO scenes and the mini games are good. I do wish there was more HO scenes and that the mini games were harder (the easiest one took me 3 clicks).

[b]Agent Walker - Secret Journey[/b] takes us to a deadly secretive mission of tracking and recovering the Spear of Destiny. Such powerful object holds a tremendous mystical power, enough to end the second world war. In a final attempt to avoid such powerful artifact of falling in the wrong hands, Agent Walker will adventure herself on the unknown. 
Right after discovering the Spear of Destiny, she's betrayed, by her comrades. The race begins, as we must track and re-possess the artifact to avoid the imminent disaster. The year is 1942, and France is under the enemy control, but the resistance is still very much alive, and with the help of some good people, there's hope till the end.

Many may know this game with a different title; [b]Spear of Destiny: The Final Journey[/b]. Although it's the same game, [i]Big Fish Games[/i] and [i]Steam[/i] use different names for the same game. This could be due to licencing regarding the game.

Published by [i]Artifex Mundi[/i] and developed by [i]Brave Giant LTD[/i], (who created titles such has the [b]Demon Hunter[/b] and [b]Queen's Quest[/b] series), we expect some good quality release, and none the less, they delivered. As the story goes, it becomes pretty simple really soon, but it's still entertaining to follow its development till the end, with a few surprises popping along the way.

As expected from [i]Brave Giant LTD[/i], the design works, areexcellent, and there are over 30 different locations, all hand drawn, that delivers the suitable atmosphere accordingly.
Even with the war reflecting upon the skies, French streets are still beautiful, magic and resisting the oppression, with the great classic style of the 40's. Across the story one will enjoy different locations such as; secret pathways, forbiddendocks, a small town, a mysterious mansion, and many others, all with small details to make your journey more appealing.
Some effects are present, such as lights and other small tweaks to enlight small design works, fancy enough to give illusions of grandeur.
The game is full 2D, as usual from the publisher, but some cutscenes deliver full 3D visuals, and it's definitely refreshing to the eyes.

[b]Agent Walker: Secret Journey[/b] runs in HD, with a beautiful 1080p resolution (compatible with lower resolutions as well), this obviously brings Hidden Object Scenes to a different level of amusement. Beyond the traditional sense, the player has also a few other smaller and interactive Hidden Object scenes, where one must unlock new items as new ones are being found. These intuitive small scenes are enjoyable and interesting, as they break from the traditional element of simply finding an object.
The puzzles are available as always, and their difficulty range from easy to medium. They tend to progressively become harder, but they never become an issue, and it's a fantastic way to introduce new players to the genre. Players more experience, can still enjoy the casual puzzles that have certainly seen in previous games.
Four levels of difficulty are present, from easy to expert, and an extra one to customize your difficulty, which is always inspected, but not welcome in these type of games.
If Hidden Objects and puzzles are a way too simple, then during this adventure, you can also collect several objects hidden across the locations, belonging to different sets such as Ships, Cloths, Airplanes, Bombs, and others. Upon gathering all of them, a few short clips become available, portraying real-life events of WW2.
[b]Agent Walker: Secret Journey[/b] offers between 3 and 4 hours of gameplay depending on your experience, more if reliability becomes an option of course! As in many other Artifex Mundi titles, Steam Cloud is available.

The soundtrack is minimalistic at best, with a piano track throughout the entire game with some changes along the way. it's a good track for ambient, in particular, when facing Hidden Object scenes. A few more tracks would bring different feelings to the adventure.
The voice acting is decent enough, and the characters show a french accent, as the militia uses a german one, to bring realism to the table.

[b]Agent Walker: Secret Journey[/b] is a medium-length adventure, with an interesting plot, but short of what could have been done. Improvements with the plot would have been a major asset.
Perfect for anyone who's new at this genre, or looking to start. Collecting Steam achievements may also be an incentive, as they are simple and fun.Overall, it's a good enough adventure, especially if purchase on special sale!

Sort of hesitant to recommend it, because I did enjoy it, but I wouldnt recommend anyone buying it at full price.

The story is set in 1942 during the war, and you are tasked with trying to find and destroy the Spear of Destiny. I loved the loose war theme (outside of some soldiers, you cant really tell theres much of a war though), and the setting was beautiful.

The storyline itself was a bit weak. It felt rushed and a bit bland. We never learn much about the protagonist, other than her mission. I think if they had expanded on the history of the Spear itself, or explored more about the protagonist/her mission, it could have been an amazing story.

Graphics were beautiful, and the animations during the cut scenes were pretty well done, especially for a hidden object game. The hidden object scenes were beautifully drawn, as were all the locations. I cant fault the game graphically at all.

Audio wasnt the greatest. The music was alright...but it got extremely repetitive. The voice actors werent the best either. Some sounded like they were literally reading directly from a script with no emoting, no matter the situation. It took away from the immersion. I ended up just turning the audio off completely.

The hidden object scenes were very well done, as were most of the puzzles, but some of the puzzles needed better explainations, or at least be reworded so they made better sense of what to do. There were a few unique puzzles which was nice to see (unfortunately, those were the ones that needed better explainations).

There are achieves, and theyre fairly easy to get, but they got a bit carried away with collectibles. Especially since, while you can fast travel to previous locations, some become "locked" once you leave, so if you miss one, you need to replay.

Overall, Id recommend it on sale, or if youre really that interested, but I cant tell anyone to buy it full price.

Usually I love Artifex Mundi games, but this is quite a sad exception. I saw the mixed reviews but as I've played others with mixed reviews before and got it on a big discount. But while the others just were not up to the usual Artifex Mundi standards and maybe somewhat boring, it's hard for me to find anything worth to play for in this game. Actually I even was deeply offended by quite some elements of this game.

Sure, you will have some hidden object games and some mini games and collecting items. But there is only a very shallow story so thin, that I am hesitant to call it even a story when thinking of so many other gems of Artifex Mundi. 

Also what you get as a story is quite often just directly violent, without a lot of explanation why. You'll have to kill people who didn't act badly as such beside of being on the other side during a war. And you have to do it multiple times and with quite some brutal solutions. This is surely not why I chose to play hidden object, puzzle, artful and story rich games.

But worse, the art is just a weird mix of some times and areas and the landscape is just put together in a very unrelated fashion, where you have to scratch your head about how these places should be connected in a sensible manner. And why are there random Egyptian or Chinese symbols in a European WW II setting?

Then why did they chose WW II as context when it's just some background and then they mix a lot of stereotype figures who in an odd fashion, where those NPCs seem to have some deeper agenda by themselves but we just use them for our needs and leave them to their own fate.

If a game is not seriously about WW II it should not use this theme. It's nothing to just play around with. As a German I really cannot understand why this was done. Without actually putting the characters in a real context regarding that war. 

But while the characters are more or less unrelated all the collections are WW II related. It's all military stuff. You have to collect uniforms and weapons. And as a reward you can watch short films about how those weapons were used. 

Seriously? Why? Why is there even more random violence show? Violence that is not based on the story of the game?

Regarding the atmosphere it doesn't really feel WW II related most of the time. It's just about two or three places that are placed accordingly. Everything else is random caves, mythtical tunnels, temples, a cellar, a random throne room, some magical green house and the like. With more or less random decorations.

The music really got to my nerves. It was not pleasing but also not really helping the story. Instead it felt extremely short repetitive.

The mini games are also mostly quite randomly placed and only seldomly there is some reason for why it's needed beside of opening one door after another. At the end it's mostly only hidden object games. Those where you have to wait for something to turn another shape again. And where you just have to search the whole place for the pointer to switch over, as you have to move a random object behind which the object you search is completely hidden. Which is also quite annoying.

Overall I find it hard to find any aspect that is well executed in this game. But to be honest, the only positive I can think about is that it's an Artifex Mundi game and if you have played all of their other games and just are desparate for another one, you could consider it. But even then I fear a lot of people would be disappointed.
It's not a bad game, but it's not up to Artifex Mundi's normally excellent standard. I wish there'd been more to the story. Perhaps consider getting it on sale if you want to complete your collection

It's standard HO fare, to be honest. The story relies heavily on fantasy and magic (because that seems to be the only way HO games can have a story.). Beautifully hand-drawn graphics, ambient music, good quantity of HO puzzles, the minigames aren't too bad, etc. etc. But the game becomes annoying for the many reasons why a lot of HO games become annoying.

The voice acting is dreadful. Unfortunately, it falls into the many shortcomings that HO games have. The people are NOT professional voice actors (which is not utterly surprising), but the accents are just .... bad.  Really, REALLY bad. Dick van Dyke did a better Cockney in "Mary Poppins" than whoever played the French woman did a French accent.  When your accent is upstaged by Dick van Dyke's Bert, that's saying something ... something really bad. And of course they have to have a woman try to play a child's voice, which is one of the most frustrating things that these HO games will do.

Unfortunately, the designers decided to do something that I ABSOLUTELY DESPISE, which is have some of the items that you're looking for *during the HO games* fade in and out, sometimes in very dark areas of the screen - and this happens on *every* HO game. KNOCK. THIS. OFF. Put the items on the screen. None of this fade-in-fade-out crap!! 

Plus every HO game has hidden items where you have to move things out of the way, but ANY misclick on an item to move means that you lose out on the "No Mistakes Allowed" achievement for that game.

Then there are the glitches where you are very obviously clicking on an object but it doesn't take. Go back a little while later to that object and it registers!

And of course we have the multiple instances of improper English translations where items might be called something by definition, but their commonly-used term is not what is used, although that could also be my Yankee version of English.  A "pipette"? You mean an "eyedropper"? That's not a "divider"! It's a "drafting compass" (for drawing circles)! A divider is something that ...you know ... SEPARATES items!  There is a distinct difference between a "gem" and a "shard". OY!!

I was on the fence about this game, but because of the fade-in-fade-out and hidden-under-something on every single HO game, I'm knocking this down to a negative vote because it's really frustrating. Play this if you must, but keep your expectations really low and expect to get frustrated at times.

Agent Walker: Secret Journey takes us into the German-occupied French countryside during World War II, where we have to recover and destroy the Spear of Destiny. The setting is quite unusual for a hidden object game and the location is also interesting, but despite these, the game falls into mediocrity.

The game starts out pretty good with all the aforementioned countryside scenery and by us finding - surprisingly fast and easily - the sought after artifact [spoiler](which functions as a weapon as we later find it out)[/spoiler]. Then it is quickly taken away from us and throughout the rest of the game we'll spend our time tracking it down. The nearby French town is a beautiful sight as well, but after a short boat trip (which is executed through a set of minigames) we'll be crawling around in dungeons and in a pretty dull castle.

The minigames are fine and there are some clever item related puzzles, like the one where we have to stuff a sack and place it under a lamp post, so the bottle placed on it (how did it get there?) won't shatter, when we knock it off. This however only applies to the first half of the game, because after we manage to leave the town, the quality of these puzzles also deteriorate. Not their numbers however, which seem to increase as we progress, but this concerns the hidden objects scenes only and this is where we get to the Achilles' heel of HOGs: the overused hidden object scenes, the ones we have to go back to twice or even three times without any hints (if played on expert difficulty). Seriously, it's better just to have the necessary items placed somewhere along the way, than reusing the same hidden object scenes over and over. The other annyoing element is the morphing object element: it's fun to use them from time to time, but when we have to wait for the third or the fourth time in a single scene for the actual item to turn into the one we need, it gets quite bothersome and time-wasting.
There are also hidden relics we can find (they aren't mandatory and are there only for achievements) such as figurines of WWII leaders, uniforms, and models of war machines. These miniature war machines are usually quite hard to spot since some of them tend to be at very abnormal locations, not to mention that they can be turned upside down too (very hard to find a battleship model for example, when it looks like a stick in standing position). Fortunately the game is forgiving enough, so the miniature collectibles we collected will be stored and we only have to look for the remaining ones in a next playthrough. (By the way the 'Fast Tapper' achievement's description is wrong, we have to find 5 items - instead of 3 - in a hidden object puzzle in 5 seconds.)

Since violence is usually very mild in hidden object games it should be noted that in this one sometimes we have to kill other human beings (soldiers actually). There's no blood of course and the situations kind of require that we should deal with our enemies this way, but still, it looks awkward to spare the life of predators, but kill humans without remorse. The only reason I mention this is because these games are usually family friendly (even though I prefer the ones with horror involved :)).

As mentioned before the graphics is nice for a hidden object game, at least for most of the time. Both the countryside and the town areas look great, it's a shame we don't get to see more of these locations. The castle where the endgame takes place is ordinary-, some might say boring looking. Also the captain's character model was reused from Demon Hunter: Chronicles from Beyond, but I'm not complaining, it's a pretty authentic looking captain :)

The music is a mixture of lethargic and annoying scores, which is strange, because other Artifex Mundi games usually have relaxing ones, which at times I'd listen to separately without playing the game itself. The voiceovers are awkward too for some of the characters: the kid in the caves sounded like a girl and a ghost in addition to that (maybe he [b]was[/b] a ghost?). Something I loved was the chirping of the birds (though it only appeared in the rare countryside/forest areas obviously).

Agent Walker: Secret Journey treads in the footsteps of Demon Hunter 1 and 2: while isn't particularly bad, it's not a game I would recommend. Artifex Mundi has so many great titles one can choose from, that this game can only fit in the runners-up section. I really hope the developer's next game will be a better one.

PROS
+ nice, colourful scenery (at least in the first half of the game)
+ some interesting item related puzzles
+ unusual setting for a HOG

CONS
- repetitious hidden object scenes and morphing objects
- languid plot
- dull second half
- annoying music

RATING
4/10

Somehow this turned out to be a weirdly hard Mundi game for me, I am not sure if it was the direction or the puzzles but my god i got stuck a LOT playing this game and not in a way that made a ton of sense. Like most of what other people have said already, this is not a well-made game. The hidden object aspect is very easy which can be good or bad depending on your preference. The puzzles, on the other hand, is a mixed bag. I've gotten stuck several times because the instructions didn't explain properly enough. The puzzles themselves are straightforward enough but the lack of clarity in instructions bumps up the difficulty level in an unsatisfying way. 
I don't generally care too much about story in HO games because they tend to be lacklustre anyway. That being said, this game definitely takes the cake in how bare-boned a "story" can be.

As often with one shot, there is an attempt to condense the whole story in a limited time with as many puzzles as possibles. The result is often meh at best and this one doesn't make exception.
This one has its own CON though, and a little PRO that others don't usually share.

PRO:
- Interesting interactions with the achivements.

CON:
- Puzzles simplified to the point they aren't puzzles anymore. Example: The poor 6 pieces puzzles.
- Some puzzles are also only follow the instructions hidden somewhere. Example: The boat where you're told that you need to follow the map on the top left, while in fact you just have to click on the grass to read the instructions.
- You often look for stuff to move around without actually knowing why you do so. Example: at some point you need to load a canon, but you have absolutely no idea what is the goal as there is nothing around that gives you an hint, until you are done and break a pole you're then using as a bridge.
- Attempt to stretch the lenght artificially.

At some point, the game itself give up, you give a toy to a little girl and she just give back another item while saying thank you. There is no backstory to that beside the fact she's scared.
I don't recommend this game unless you like WWII History, that it's your very first HOG or you want to gift it to a kid.
